sections.skill: Identify the task, context, audience and purpose a request needs

questions.domain: Foundation 4: Asking for what you need
questions.prompt: In "Explain (the action word) photosynthesis (the process) to a group of eight-year-olds," which part names the audience?

choices.text: to
photosynthesis (the process)
Explain (the action word)
a group of eight-year-olds

questions.correct_answer: a group of eight-year-olds
questions.intro: A useful request (often called a PROMPT) usually covers four things. The TASK: what you want done ("write," "compare," "list," "explain"). The CONTEXT: background the tool cannot know, such as your situation, the facts involved or what you already tried. The AUDIENCE: who will read or use the result, such as a ten-year-old, a manager or yourself. The PURPOSE: why you need it, such as to persuade, to decide or to study. A vague request like "write about recycling" leaves the tool to guess all four, so the result may be generic. Adding the missing pieces gives it a fair chance.
questions.feedback: The audience is who will read or use it.

sections.skill: Separate a request from the background it needs

questions.domain: Foundation 4: Asking for what you need
questions.prompt: In "make dinner," what is missing?

choices.text: The background, such as allergies
The house address
The request itself
The babysitter's full name and age

questions.correct_answer: The background, such as allergies
questions.intro: Imagine asking a new babysitter to "make dinner." That is a REQUEST, but the babysitter does not know the BACKGROUND: one child is allergic to nuts, dinner is at 6, and the kids love pasta. Without that background, the babysitter might make something unsafe or unwanted. An AI tool is similar. The request says what to do; the background, or context, says what the tool cannot see for itself. Good results need both, but a request alone often feels complete to the person asking, because they already know the background.
questions.feedback: The background is missing.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Find the missing or conflicting piece before sending

questions.domain: Foundation 4: Asking for what you need
questions.prompt: "Explain this contract simply for my grandmother, in full legal detail." What is the problem?

choices.text: Grandmothers cannot read contracts
It asks for two different audiences at once
It is too short to be understood at all
It does not say what the contract is about

questions.correct_answer: It asks for two different audiences at once
questions.intro: Sometimes a request seems complete but the pieces pull against each other, or one key detail is assumed rather than stated. "Explain this contract simply for my grandmother, in full legal detail" asks for two different audiences at once. "Fix the schedule" assumes the tool knows which schedule and what is wrong with it. Before sending an important request, reread it as a stranger would: could someone with no background do exactly what you want? If not, add or fix the missing piece first.
questions.feedback: Simple-for-a-grandmother and full legal detail conflict.
